content: Nevus depigmentosus, also known as nevus achromicus, is a condition characterized by localized depigmentation of the skin. It is distinct from vitiligo and can be easily differentiated from it. While age does not play a significant role in the development of nevus depigmentosus, approximately 19% of cases are noted at birth. The size of the depigmented patches may increase proportionally with the growth of the body, but their distribution remains stable, and the lesions are non-progressive hypopigmented patches. Individuals with nevus depigmentosus are more susceptible to sunburn due to the lack of pigment in the affected areas. It is essential for patients to use effective sun protection measures, including the application of sunscreen to all exposed skin. This not only prevents sunburn but also reduces the contrast between hypopigmented and normal skin by minimizing tanning of the unaffected areas. Most patients with nevus depigmentosus do not seek treatment for their lesions, as there is currently no method to repigment the affected skin. For those with cosmetic concerns, camouflage makeup can be an effective option. In cases where the lesion is small, surgical excision may be considered. The exact cause of nevus depigmentosus remains unclear. It is hypothesized to result from a sporadic defect during embryonic development. Although it has been described as localized albinism, this characterization is inaccurate. The hypopigmented spots in nevus depigmentosus are due to abnormalities in the function of melanocytes, which produce insufficient pigment, leading to the appearance of white spots on the skin. Nevus depigmentosus must be differentiated from vitiligo during diagnosis. On physical examination, the lesions appear as localized white spots that can occur on any part of the body. These lesions are stable and do not progress over time. In most cases, the lesions are not completely achromic but are hypopigmented and resemble splashes of paint. If hair is present in the affected area, it is often colorless or white. The individual lesions are permanent. There are no effective therapies for repigmenting the skin in nevus depigmentosus. Various therapeutic approaches, such as PUVA (psoralen + UVA treatment), excimer laser therapy, and grafting techniques, have been attempted. However, PUVA therapy has not demonstrated any significant benefit. While repigmentation through grafting techniques is possible, the results are inconsistent, and recurrence of the depigmentation is a potential issue. Based on the experiences of other researchers and clinicians, the quality and retention of pigment following treatment are unpredictable. These factors should be carefully considered when consulting with and offering treatment options to patients with nevus depigmentosus.
